page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b) 'per-request memory budget' and §8 mini-case bullet 2
quoted_clause: the ~436 GB KV budget (640 − 140 − 64, §3(b)) supports ~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K-token requests per host before KV pressure
observed: The chapter states the canonical workload's arrival rate (~10 rps average, §3(a)) and its own end-to-end latency (TTFT ~1.2 s + decode ~7.5 s at 25 ms TPOT, §8 mini-case), but never checks the two against the single-host configuration it recommends. Little's law on the chapter's own numbers gives concurrency = 10 rps × ~8.7 s ≈ 87 in-flight requests; at ~24.1 GB KV each that is ≈ 2.1 TB of KV, i.e. ≈ 5 hosts at 436 GB KV/host. Equivalently, the per-host KV ceiling of ~18 concurrent requests caps the host at 18 / 8.7 s ≈ 2.1 rps — roughly one fifth of the canonical 10 rps. The mini-case nevertheless closes with 'the 70B FP16 base model for the generation leg ... served on 8×H100 with vLLM continuous batching' as the shortlist, and §3(b) asserts 'This is comfortably within a single 8×H100 node's capacity' (true for one request, false for the workload).
evidence: Recomputed from the chapter's own printed values: 9,200 + 300 = 9,500 tokens/request; KV/request = 9,200 × 2.62 MB = 24.1 GB; per-host KV = 640 − 140 − 64 = 436 GB; 436 / 24.1 = 18.1 requests; end-to-end = 1.2 s + 300 × 0.025 s = 8.7 s; required concurrency = 10 × 8.7 = 87; required KV = 87 × 24.1 GB = 2,097 GB; hosts = 2,097 / 436 = 4.8. Throughput ceiling of one host = 18 / 8.7 s = 2.07 rps < 10 rps.
root_cause: The worked example sizes a single request against the host and then treats the resulting host count as the answer, without ever closing the loop to the canonical arrival rate. The mini-case also silently drops the ~10 rps figure, so the contradiction is invisible at the point where the shortlist is declared.
correction: Add an explicit capacity closure to §3(b) (or the mini-case): state the canonical arrival rate, derive required concurrency via Little's law, derive required KV and host count, and either (a) show that the canonical workload needs N hosts and revise the 'one 8×H100 host' framing, or (b) state explicitly that the single-host figure is a per-host unit of analysis and that the fleet-level closure is deferred to the capacity/fleet chapters with a pointer. The mini-case bullet should carry the ~10 rps figure so the reader can see the closure.
acceptance_test: A reader can compute, from the chapter alone, the number of hosts required to serve the canonical 10 rps at the stated SLOs, and the chapter's stated host count matches that number (or the chapter explicitly says the count is per-host and names the chapter where the fleet closure occurs). No sentence in Ch 5 asserts that one 8×H100 host serves the canonical 10 rps workload.

quoted_clause: [canonical scenario][DERIVED] KV cache cost per token at FP16: for a Llama‑style 70B model, n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, bytes per element = 2 (FP16). KV cache per token = n_layers × 2 × d_model × bytes = 80 ×2 × 8192 ×2 = 2,621,440 bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token
observed: The arithmetic is a full-MHA computation (K and V each at d_model = 8192), but it is attributed to a 'Llama-style 70B model'. Every widely deployed Llama-2/Llama-3 70B uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads of head_dim 128, i.e. n_kv_dim = 1024, not 8192. For such a model the KV footprint per token is 80 × 2 × 1024 × 2 = 327,680 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB/token — 8× smaller than the figure printed here. The book's canonical KV figure is (correctly, per house convention) the full-MHA reference; the defect is the model attribution, which invites the reader to believe a real Llama-70B deployment needs 24.1 GB of KV per 9.2K request.
evidence: Llama-2 70B: 80 layers, hidden 8192, 64 attention heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 → KV dim = 8 × 128 = 1024. Full-MHA reference: 80 × 2 × 8192 × 2 = 2,621,440 B = 2.62 MB/token (as printed). GQA-8 reference: 80 × 2 × 1024 × 2 = 327,680 B = 0.328 MB/token; 9,200 tokens → 3.0 GB, not 24.1 GB.
root_cause: The canonical teaching geometry is a synthetic full-MHA 70B, but the prose names a real, GQA-based model family as its source, conflating the constructed geometry with a real checkpoint.
correction: Rename the reference explicitly, e.g. 'for the canonical full-MHA 70B reference (n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, no GQA — the constructed teaching geometry of Ch 4 Table 4-2)', and add one sentence noting that a real Llama-2/3 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads and therefore has ~0.33 MB/token at FP16, i.e. ~8× less KV — which is exactly the GQA effect the book teaches elsewhere. Keep the 2.62 MB/token canonical value unchanged so downstream chapters stay consistent.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 5 attributes the 2.62 MB/token full-MHA figure to a real Llama checkpoint; the text states the full-MHA assumption explicitly and states the GQA-8 alternative with its 8× factor.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b) '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: tokens/s per dollar with prefill included'
quoted_clause: under continuous batching (prefill of one request overlapping decode of another), on a combined prefill+decode basis the same host moves 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s ≈ 285,000 tokens/$ (one hour of host time at that rate); the single-stream floor is 9,500/7.08 ≈ 1,342 tok/s ≈ 242,000 tokens/$ (one hour of host time)
observed: The 1,583 tok/s figure is not a host throughput rate. It is the decode rate multiplied by the tokens-per-request ratio, i.e. it assumes each request's entire 9,200-token prefill is absorbed inside the 6.0 s of decode time. But the chapter itself states prefill of one request takes ~1.08 s of GPU time and that the host's prefill rate is ~8,518 tok/s (9,200 ÷ 1.08 s). If prefill and decode overlap, the host's combined rate is the sum of the two concurrent rates (≈ 8,518 + 50 ≈ 8,568 tok/s if prefill-bound), not the product of the decode rate with the token ratio; if they do not overlap, the rate is the serial 9,500 / 7.08 = 1,342 tok/s. The two printed figures therefore differ by a method error, not by a batching effect, and the paragraph's own conclusion ('The per-dollar figures therefore scale up substantially at batch') is supported by a number that is not a throughput at all. The 285,000 tokens/$ figure is also not comparable to the 9,000 tokens/$ figure in Table 5-2 (output tokens only) without an explicit basis statement.
evidence: Serial: (9,200 + 300) / (1.08 + 6.0) = 9,500 / 7.08 = 1,341.8 tok/s → × 3600 / $20 = 241,500 tokens/$ (as printed). Overlapped: 9,200 / 1.08 = 8,518 tok/s prefill + 50 tok/s decode = 8,568 tok/s → × 3600 / $20 = 1,542,000 tokens/$. The printed 1,583 tok/s equals 50 × 31.67, which is a token-equivalent rate with no time basis. The printed pair (1,583 vs 1,342) differs by 18%, which is inconsistent with the text's claim that batching scales the figure up 'substantially'.
root_cause: A token-count ratio was substituted for a time-based rate. The paragraph mixes a per-request token accounting with a host-level throughput accounting without stating the concurrency at which the host is saturated.
correction: Replace the 1,583 tok/s derivation with a time-based one. State the concurrency C at which the host is evaluated and compute the combined rate as min-bound by prefill and decode resources: e.g. at C concurrent requests, decode contributes C × 50 tok/s and prefill contributes up to 8,518 tok/s, so the combined rate is min(C × 50 + 8,518, ...) subject to the KV ceiling of ~18 concurrent requests. If the intent is to keep the single-stream figure, say so and drop the 1,583 number. Also state explicitly that 9,000 tokens/$ (output only) and the combined tokens/$ are different metrics and must not be compared directly.
acceptance_test: Every tokens/s figure in §3(b) is derived from a stated time basis and a stated concurrency; the combined prefill+decode rate is reproducible from the printed prefill rate and decode rate; no figure in the chapter is produced by multiplying a token ratio by a token rate.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'
quoted_clause: the bge‑large‑en option is not justified at this scale: its quality gain over all‑mpnet‑base‑v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics), and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64‑token embedding in the table above, the same ratio as their parameter counts) — validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it.
observed: The chapter applies a decision rule to bge-large that it does not apply to the recommendation it actually makes. bge-large is rejected because its quality gain over mpnet is unquantified and would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar. The identical argument applies to the recommended mpnet over MiniLM: the quality gain is equally unquantified for that pair, and the bar is ~4.8× FLOP (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP), which is larger. The chapter nevertheless recommends mpnet, on the strength of a 'few to ~15% MAP' prior that is explicitly labeled an unverified hypothesis and is not tied to this model pair. The recommendation therefore rests on a weaker evidential basis than the one used to reject the alternative, and the stated criterion is applied asymmetrically.
evidence: Table 5-1 rows: MiniLM 2.94 GFLOP, mpnet 14.08 GFLOP, bge-large 42.88 GFLOP per 64-token query. Ratios: mpnet/MiniLM = 4.79×; bge/mpnet = 3.05×. The text's own quality evidence for mpnet over MiniLM is 'an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS]', i.e. no pair-specific measurement — the same status as the bge gain it rejects.
root_cause: The recommendation was fixed before the criterion was applied, and the criterion was then used only to remove alternatives rather than to test the recommendation.
correction: Apply the bar symmetrically. Either (a) state the recommendation as a provisional shortlist entry explicitly conditional on a measured ΔMAP ≥ the stated threshold (with the threshold written as a MAP-per-FLOPS or MAP-per-storage figure so the reader can compute it), or (b) present the three candidates as a shortlist with the decision deferred to the §7 validation, and remove the word 'recommended' from Table 5-2's 'Selection status' row in favor of 'provisional shortlist, pending target-corpus validation'. If the recommendation is retained, the text must say why the ~4.8× bar is cleared while the ~3× bar is not.
acceptance_test: The same evidential standard (measured or explicitly hypothesized pair-specific quality gain vs. a stated FLOP/storage bar) is applied to every candidate in Table 5-1, including the recommended one; the recommendation's justification is either a measurement or an explicitly stated assumption that is flagged as load-bearing.

quoted_clause: reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower storage and compute — e.g. a 384‑dim variant of the same model family can halve the index storage of a 768‑dim one (the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged, since only the final projection shrinks)
observed: The paragraph's headline claims a compute saving from reducing dimension, then states in the same sentence that the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged. The two statements are only reconcilable if 'reducing dimension' means post-hoc truncation or Matryoshka-style training of one model at multiple output widths — in which case there is no compute saving at all, only a storage saving. The compute saving the chapter actually quantifies later (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP) comes from choosing a smaller model (MiniLM vs mpnet), which is a model-size change, not a dimension change. The paragraph conflates the two, and the parenthetical 'only the final projection shrinks' describes truncation, not a trained 384-dim variant, which would have a smaller encoder.
evidence: Table 5-1: MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim, ~23M) vs all-mpnet-base-v2 (768-dim, ~110M) differ in encoder depth/width, not only in output dimension; the 4.8× FLOP gap is a parameter-count gap. The table's own footnote already separates the two effects ('the proxy overstates compute most for the smallest model').
root_cause: Two distinct interventions (truncating a fixed model's output width; substituting a smaller model) are described with one vocabulary ('dimension'), so the compute claim inherits the wrong referent.
correction: Split the claim into two: (i) truncating or Matryoshka-training a fixed encoder to a lower output width reduces index storage and query-time projection cost but leaves encoder compute essentially unchanged; (ii) substituting a smaller encoder reduces both storage and compute, and is a model-selection decision, not a dimension decision. Then state which of the two the ~4.8× FLOP figure belongs to.
acceptance_test: The §3(a) dimension paragraph and the Table 5-1 footnote use the same distinction, and the 4.8× FLOP figure is attributed to model size rather than to output dimension.

quoted_clause: It is only **~15% of the wall-clock time** (1.08 s prefill vs 6.0 s decode) ... vs. at 300 output tokens and ~25 ms TPOT, decode alone is ~7.5 s versus ~1.08 s prefill
observed: The chapter uses two different batch-1 decode rates for the same canonical workload: 50 tok/s (20 ms/token, 6.0 s for 300 tokens) in §3(b), and 25 ms/token (40 tok/s, 7.5 s for 300 tokens) in the mini-case. The economics unit note acknowledges that 50 tok/s is an illustrative low-batch point above the canonical 40 tok/s, but the mini-case then silently switches to the canonical rate and presents 7.5 s without labeling the switch, so the reader sees two different decode durations for one workload with no marker at the point of use. The derived wall-clock shares also differ (85% vs 87%) and the per-request economics (9,000 tokens/$) are computed from the 50 tok/s point while the latency narrative in the mini-case uses 40 tok/s.
evidence: §3(b): 300 tokens ÷ 50 tok/s = 6.0 s; 1.08 / (1.08 + 6.0) = 15.3%. Mini-case: 300 × 0.025 s = 7.5 s; 7.5 / (7.5 + 1.08) = 87.4%. Both are internally consistent; the defect is the unannounced change of rate between them.
root_cause: The reconciliation note was placed in the economics paragraph rather than at the point where the second rate is used, so the mini-case inherits a number whose provenance is not visible there.
correction: Use one canonical decode rate for the chapter's worked example (the canonical 25 ms/token / 40 tok/s from Ch 2) and treat 50 tok/s as a clearly labeled sensitivity variant, or carry the [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label into the mini-case bullet. If both rates must appear, state in the mini-case which rate is in use and why.
acceptance_test: Every decode-duration figure in Ch 5 is either the canonical 25 ms/token or carries an explicit [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] label at the point of use; the chapter contains no unlabeled second decode rate.

quoted_clause: the system is first-order memory‑capacity‑bound (the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit — KV HBM capacity limits concurrency, not bandwidth — at the Ch 17 concurrency screen)
observed: The chapter's own concurrency arithmetic (the 436 GB KV budget and the ~18-request screen) is attributed to Ch 7 elsewhere in the same chapter ('the ~64 GB runtime reserve that the concurrency budget in Ch. 7 subtracts to reach the ~436 GB KV budget'). Pointing the reader to Ch 17 for the concurrency screen is therefore either a stale reference from an earlier structure or a reference to a chapter whose concurrency content is not the screen described. Either way the reader is sent to the wrong place for the one concept the paragraph is trying to establish.
evidence: Internal inconsistency within Ch 5: §2 cites Ch 17 for the concurrency screen; §3(b) cites Ch 7 for the concurrency budget that produces the same 436 GB figure.
root_cause: Cross-reference drift after a chapter move, with no automated check on chapter-number references.
correction: Verify the intended target and correct the reference to the chapter that actually derives the KV concurrency screen (Ch 7 per §3(b)), or, if Ch 17 does contain a fleet-level concurrency screen, cite both with a one-clause distinction ('per-host screen in Ch 7; fleet-level screen in Ch 17').
acceptance_test: Every chapter cross-reference in Ch 5 resolves to a chapter that contains the cited material; a reader following the §2 reference finds the concurrency screen, not a different topic.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b) opening and §8 mini-case closing paragraph
quoted_clause: The architect must decide whether a base 70B‑class dense model, a smaller dense model, or a fine‑tuned variant best satisfies the latency, quality, and economic constraints.

The MoE rejection appears only in the mini-case, as an assertion, with no arithmetic.

Show which SLOs each fails or passes. If the MoE rejection is asserted in the mini-case, back it with the weight-residency arithmetic there or move it into §3(b).

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) first [HYPOTHESIS] paragraph and §3(a) 'The decision hinges on...'
quoted_clause: Any observed quality‑vs‑dimension relationship (reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference) is domain‑ and corpus‑specific and must be validated on the target corpus.
observed: A quantitative empirical range ('a few to ~15% MAP') is asserted with no citation, and it is then used twice as the load-bearing quality prior for the chapter's recommendation ('the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain'). The [HYPOTHESIS] label correctly marks it as unverified, but the book elsewhere distinguishes 'unverified because no measurement exists' from 'unverified because the measurement has not been done yet'; here published reports are said to exist ('reports range from...') yet none is cited, so the reader cannot check the range, its metric definition (MAP@10? MAP over what corpus?), or its direction. The same range is restated as 'an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS]' in the takeaway, where it becomes the justification for the recommendation.
evidence: No footnote or reference accompanies the range in either location; the chapter's other empirical claims (H100 memory, price, engine behavior) are footnoted or explicitly labeled.
root_cause: A quantitative prior was introduced to make the recommendation decidable without sourcing the literature it claims to summarize.
correction: Either cite the specific studies behind the range (with metric definition, corpus, and year) and scope the claim to them, or restate the range as an explicit scenario assumption with no claim that published reports exist — e.g. 'assume a quality uplift of up to 15% MAP for the larger model; this is a scenario input, not a measurement'. Then make the recommendation's dependence on that input explicit.
acceptance_test: Every numeric quality range in Ch 5 is either footnoted to a specific source with metric and corpus, or is labeled as a scenario assumption without an implied literature.

quoted_clause: | Tokens per dollar (generation, runtime) | 9,000 tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |

Two other tokens-per-dollar figures appear in the same chapter (≈242,000 and ≈285,000 tokens/$ on a combined prefill+decode basis), so a reader comparing Table 5-2 with §3(b) sees an apparent 26–32× discrepancy that is a metric-basis difference, not a finding. The table is the most likely place a reader will copy a number from.

Keep the two rows adjacent so the basis difference is visible at a glance.

quoted_clause: (~200 GFLOP/s is the AVX‑512 theoretical peak, not a sustained rate)
observed: A specific per-core peak is stated as fact without a source or a machine description. A 200 GFLOP/s AVX-512 per-core peak requires roughly 3.1 GHz with two 512-bit FMA units; mainstream server cores land nearer 120–160 GFLOP/s. The number is used only to characterize the gap to sustained rates, so the conclusion is insensitive to it, but the parenthetical reads as a specification.

page_hint: Ch 5, §1 'Inference mode is a candidate, not a selection verdict'
quoted_clause: AR fill-in-the-middle (FIM) models — autoregressive models trained to infill a marked span — are a necessary editing baseline.

The chapter's own framing elsewhere is careful to scope claims to workloads, so this reads as an overreach.
evidence: No source; the claim is not workload-scoped in the sentence.
root_cause: A recommendation from a specific editing workflow was generalized to a class of tasks.
correction: Soften to a workload-scoped statement, e.g. 'for code-editing workloads where only a span changes, an FIM-trained model is the natural baseline to compare against, because it avoids re-generating unchanged context'.
acceptance_test: No unqualified necessity claim survives in Ch 5; each is scoped to a named workload class.

quoted_clause: supports ~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K‑token requests per host before KV pressure
observed: The concurrency screen divides the KV budget by the initial (prefill-only) KV footprint, but each request continues to grow its KV during decode: 300 output tokens add 300 × 2.62 MB ≈ 0.79 GB, so the steady-state footprint is ≈ 24.9 GB and the true ceiling is ≈ 17.5 requests. correction: Add the derivation inline: '0.98 × 0.53125 B (MXFP4: 4 bits + 8-bit scale per 32 elements) + 0.02 × 2 B (BF16) = 0.5606 B/param; 2 ÷ 0.5606 ≈ 3.567 FLOP/B', or cross-reference the exact Ch 7 derivation.
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 3.567 from the printed inputs alone, or the number is replaced by a pointer to the Ch 7 derivation.

quoted_clause: decode intensity ≈ batch size (weight-only), so at batch=32 the effective intensity is ~32 FLOP/byte

With attention included, the weight-only intensity is ≈1.17 × batch, not ≈ batch. The two numerators are used without being distinguished.

root_cause: Two FLOP conventions (linear-only vs linear+attention) coexist in one subsection without a stated rule for which applies where.

The derivation is one line and would strengthen the point (the per-GPU stream rate is ~21% of that GPU's HBM bandwidth, i.e. bandwidth is not the binding constraint at TP=8 — which is itself a useful architectural observation the paragraph does not draw).

page_hint: Ch 8 §7, 'What We Still Don't Know', bullet 3
quoted_clause: Linear attention (DeltaNet, MLA), compressed attention (CSA, HCA), and hybrid sparse patterns have different FLOP profiles and data movement.
observed: MLA (Multi-head Latent Attention) is grouped under 'linear attention'. MLA is a low-rank KV-compression mechanism: its FLOP profile and its KV footprint change because the latent cache is small and is re-expanded per step, not because attention is linear in sequence length. The grouping will mislead a reader who then reasons about MLA's roofline position using linear-attention intuition.
evidence: MLA's defining property is a c_KV-dimensional latent cache with up-projection at decode; its per-token cost is dominated by the up-projection and the cache read, and its KV footprint is a fraction of full MHA. That is a different mechanism from DeltaNet's recurrent state update.
root_cause: Mechanisms grouped by 'attention alternatives' rather than by the mechanism that determines their FLOP/byte profile.
correction: Separate them: 'Linear attention (DeltaNet) replaces the KV cache with a fixed-size recurrent state; compressed/low-rank attention (MLA) shrinks the KV cache by a rank bottleneck and adds an up-projection; sparse patterns (CSA, HCA) reduce the number of attended pairs. Each changes the FLOP/byte profile for a different reason, so their roofline positions must be derived separately.'
acceptance_test: No mechanism is grouped under a category whose defining property it does not share; MLA is discussed as a cache-compression mechanism wherever it appears.

quoted_clause: far above one host's KV-residency ceiling (C ≈ 17.5, conservative integer floor 17)
observed: The KV-residency ceiling C is quoted without derivation and cannot be reconstructed from anything in this chapter, even though the chapter supplies every input that would be needed (2.62 MB/token FP16, 9,200 tokens → 24.1 GB KV per request; 8 × 80 GB = 640 GB HBM; 140 GB of weights).
evidence: A naive reconstruction gives (640 − 140) / 24.1 ≈ 20.7 requests per host, or 640/24.1 ≈ 26.6 if weights are ignored — neither is 17.5. The 17.5 presumably reflects additional reservations (activation workspace, fragmentation, a utilization cap) that are not stated here. The reader therefore cannot tell whether C = 17.5 is a per-host figure, a per-GPU figure, or a policy-capped figure.
root_cause: A number imported from Ch 17 is used in Ch 8's scope argument without the minimum derivation needed to make it checkable.
correction: Add one line: 'C ≈ 17.5 concurrent requests per host (Ch 17: 640 GB of HBM less 140 GB of weights, less activation workspace and a utilization cap, ÷ 24.1 GB of KV per request at 9.2K)'. If the derivation genuinely lives in Ch 17, cite the specific table/equation rather than the chapter.
acceptance_test: A reader can reconstruct C from the printed inputs, or the text points to the exact Ch 17 location where C is derived.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, 'Worked Example: Canonical Scenario Arithmetic', opening paragraph
quoted_clause: the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference (a 70B-class dense model)
observed: The canonical reference's parameter count and its layer/hidden geometry are not mutually consistent under standard transformer sizing: 80 layers × d = 8192 with full MHA and an FFN ratio of 4 gives ≈12·L·d² ≈ 64.4B parameters, not 70B. The chapter uses N = 70B for the linear FLOP term and (n_layers = 80, d = 8192) for the quadratic attention term, so the two terms come from slightly different models.
evidence: 12 × 80 × 8192² = 64.4B. Reaching 70B with d = 8192 requires ~87 layers, or a wider FFN (e.g. ratio ≈ 4.7). The effect on the attention term is second-order (attention is +17% of prefill FLOPs at 9.2K), but the inconsistency is exactly the kind that a careful reader will notice and that undermines the 'one canonical model' discipline the chapter enforces elsewhere.
root_cause: The canonical reference was assembled from familiar 70B-class attributes (80 layers, d = 8192) without reconciling them against a single parameter count.
correction: State the reconciliation explicitly: either give the FFN intermediate size and note that N = 70B is a rounded class label for a 64–70B parameter geometry, or adjust n_layers to the value implied by N = 70B at d = 8192 and note the change to the attention term. Either way, add one sentence: 'N = 70B is a class label; the FLOP term uses N and the attention term uses (n_layers, d), which are not exactly self-consistent under 12·L·d² sizing — the resulting error in the attention term is under 10% at 9.2K.'
acceptance_test: The canonical model's parameter count, layer count, hidden size and FFN size are mutually consistent, or the residual inconsistency is stated and bounded.

quoted_clause: If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts)
observed: The parenthetical attributes the prefill compute-bound regime to model size. Under the chapter's own intensity model, prefill weight-only intensity is ≈ L FLOP/byte (independent of N), so the regime is set by sequence length, not parameter count. A 70B model at 100 tokens has intensity ≈100 FLOP/byte, below the 295 ridge, and would be memory-bound; a 7B model at 9,200 tokens has intensity ≈9,200 and is compute-bound.
evidence: The mini-case states the relation exactly: 'Prefill's effective intensity is (2 × N × L)/(N × 2 bytes/param) = L = 9,200 FLOP/byte'. N cancels. The §6 parenthetical therefore names the wrong variable.
root_cause: The regime label was attached to the model the chapter happens to use rather than to the quantity that determines it.
correction: Replace with: 'If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is at long context, where weight-only intensity ≈ L FLOP/byte exceeds the ridge for any model size)'. This also makes the statement transferable, which is the book's stated goal.
acceptance_test: No regime label in Ch 8 is attributed to model size where the chapter's own derivation makes it a function of sequence length.

page_hint: Ch 8 §1, 'Fewer sequential evaluations can mean more total work' vs §1, 'A resource model survives a backend change'
quoted_clause: *Implementation observations: 2026-10-28. The work counters below are illustrative, not measured performance.* ... *Backend-documentation observations: 2026-10-28. They do not establish feature availability at the edition's 2026-08-30 cutoff.*

quoted_clause: *Prefill PFLOP also grows with context: 2 ×70B × L tokens scales linearly — ~0.28 PFLOP at 2K → ~4.5 PFLOP at 32K (K = 1,000, the book's convention: 9.2K = 9,200) — so the longer the window, the larger the one-time compute cost of loading it. quoted_clause: An illustrative work model makes the distinction precise. Let `C` be fixed work outside a repeated core, `F` the work of one core pass, and `r` the executed pass count.
observed: This subsection sits between 'FLOPs per token' and 'Prefill PFLOP for 9.2K input', interrupting the canonical arithmetic that the section is named for. Its subject (repeated core passes, pass-count vs total-work accounting) is the subject of §1's 'Fewer sequential evaluations can mean more total work' subsection, with which it shares the C + rF framing.

Placing it in §3 gives the reader two explanations of the same idea in different chapters without the second advancing the first.

quoted_clause: - **Using peak TFLOP/s as sustained throughput.** ... - **Ignoring the batch-size dependence of arithmetic intensity.**
observed: The chapter's own figure caption insists that 'a kernel's position on the roofline is a *theoretical* bound on its FLOP/byte intensity — it is **not a measured latency**', but the Common Mistakes list contains no entry for the most consequential roofline misuse: treating a roofline position as a latency or throughput prediction. The list covers FLOP-count exactness, prefill/decode intensity, peak vs sustained, batch dependence, and sparsity — all real, but the latency-prediction trap is the one a solution architect actually falls into.
evidence: The chapter repeatedly warns against exactly this in captions and prose (Fig 8.2 caption; 'It is an upper-bound analysis value, not a servable goodput'; 'Actual reachable prefill throughput must come from benchmark goodput'), but a reader scanning the Common Mistakes list — the part most likely to be read and remembered — will not find it.
root_cause: The mistake list was assembled from the chapter's arithmetic topics rather than from the chapter's stated warnings.
correction: Add an entry: '**Reading a roofline position as a latency.** The roofline bounds attainable FLOP/s for a given intensity; it does not predict milliseconds. A kernel at 1 FLOP/byte on an H100 is bounded by 3.35 TB/s, but the achieved latency also depends on kernel efficiency, launch overhead, synchronization and the scheduler. Use the roofline to choose what to measure, then measure.'
acceptance_test: The Common Mistakes list contains an entry on roofline-as-latency, and its wording matches the Fig 8.2 caption's caveat.
